name: Partsy — photo to labelled exploded diagram
one_liner: For anyone holding an unfamiliar object — a flat-pack bracket, a bike derailleur, a dishwasher filter — Partsy turns one photo into a labelled exploded diagram with part names, what each part does, and the right search term to buy a replacement.
problem: Everyone has stood over a disassembled thing — a dripping tap cartridge, a stripped IKEA cam lock, a stroller wheel, a vacuum brush bar — not knowing what the parts are called. Not knowing the name is the whole blocker: you cannot search for the replacement, you cannot read the manual, you cannot ask for help. Today people take a photo and post it to r/whatisthisthing or scroll a 40-page PDF manual. Partsy is for that moment: upload one photo, get a clean exploded-style diagram with every visible part pulled apart, numbered, named, a one-line "what it does", and a copyable search string ("Bosch dishwasher lower spray arm bearing"). The surprise is seeing a messy phone snapshot become something that looks like a page from a service manual.
target_customer: Builders and makers on X (the crowd that shared the teardown skill and the IKEA-instructions video), plus DIY/repair communities: r/fixit, r/whatisthisthing, iFixit forums, bike and 3D-printer Discords. Free, no signup, open source — the audience is anyone who shares a cool before/after.
why_now: Two bookmarks this week show the primitive just landed: @jakubkrehel's /teardown skill makes agents produce editable SVG technical illustrations with annotations, and @nutlope's "never reading IKEA instructions again" clip shows multimodal models now parse physical assembly from an image. Current vision models can both identify parts in a photo and emit structured SVG in one pass, which was not reliable a year ago. Agent Skills are also mainstream now (Anthropic reported ~1M published skills in Oct 2026), so a skill-backed web version rides a live wave.
comparables: iFixit (ifixit.com) has superb human-written teardowns and a FixBot assistant, but only for devices it already covers, and it will not diagram the random bracket in your hand. BILT (bilt.ai) sells interactive 3D assembly instructions to manufacturers — enterprise, per-product, not user-photo driven. @jakubkrehel's /teardown skill (npx skills add jakubkrehel/skills) is the closest prior art, but it is a CLI skill for agent users who type an object name; Partsy is a no-install web page where the input is your own photo of a specific real object and the output includes a buy-this-part search string. Adobe Illustrator / CorelDRAW Technical Suite generate vector art from prompts but need a licence, skill and a desktop.
build_plan: Stack: single Next.js page on Vercel, TypeScript, no DB, no auth. 1) Upload or camera-capture a photo, downscale client-side. 2) One call to a multimodal model (Gemini-class or GPT-class vision) with a strict JSON schema: object guess, confidence, parts[] {name, function, approx bounding box, likely material, search_term}. 3) Second call asks the model for an SVG exploded layout using those part names, or — safer — render the diagram deterministically in SVG from the JSON: the photo as a faded base layer, numbered callout pins at the bounding boxes, parts fanned out in a legend column. 4) Interactions: hover a part to highlight the pin, click to copy its search term, toggle "annotations on/off", download SVG and PNG. 5) Share: render a 1200x630 OG card of the diagram so posted links preview the result. 6) Open source on GitHub with the prompt in the README. Cut: 3D, true geometry-accurate explosions, multi-photo reconstruction, accounts, history, any paid tier. If the model's SVG is ugly, ship the photo-plus-callouts version — it is still the screenshot people post.
launch_post:
Took a photo of a part I couldn't name and got this back.

Partsy: one photo → a labelled exploded diagram. Every part named, what it does, and the exact search term to buy a replacement.

Free, no signup, open source. Try it on the weirdest thing on your desk.
reasoning:
The build wins tonight. Three bookmarks point at the same new primitive from different angles: the /teardown skill producing editable annotated SVG, the IKEA-instructions clip, and the Grok-drag-onto-what-you're-looking-at concept — all of them are "point at a physical thing, get structure back". Partsy is the one-input-one-output version of that, which is exactly the shape of every project in the taste file (roomGPT, restorePhotos, Napkins): a photo in, a striking artefact out, free and open source, and the artefact itself is the launch post. It is not a clone of the /teardown skill: that is a CLI skill for agent users who name an object; Partsy is a no-install web page where the input is your own photo of a specific object you are holding and the output carries a buyable part name. Pain is latent — nobody says "I wish I had an exploded diagram" — so the thing that makes people notice it is the first screenshot: a phone snapshot turned into something that looks like a page from a service manual. That is why it scores high on wow and shareability and only 6 on usefulness; repeat use depends on the part names being right often enough to actually order the part. Why it could grow: the same pipeline sold to appliance and furniture brands as auto-generated spare-parts diagrams is a real B2B wedge, which is why could_grow is true. Biggest failure risk is hallucinated part names, mitigated by showing a confidence chip and framing output as "best guess, verify before buying".

The runner-up venture, Proofline, comes from the Thorsten Ball article, whose sharpest point is that he demands end-to-end proof — demo videos, before/after measurements — from agents rather than trusting them. Research shows Cursor already does video evidence internally for its background agents (Arize write-up) and Momentic sells AI QA with evidence, so the gap is narrower than it first looks; the room left is the team-level artefact for orgs merging dozens of agent PRs a week with no house standard for what counts as proof. It scores 6.6 — worth watching, not yet worth months.

Dropped as repeats or weak: an audit tool for `npx skills add` (direct repeat of Skillscope in the library); a diligence-answer drafter off the Papermark launch (direct repeat of Dossier); multi-agent observability off the Katelyn Lesse post (too close to Driftwatch/Holdroom territory and a crowded, well-funded space). Nothing here reuses a past short_name.
candidates_considered: 1) Partsy — photo to labelled exploded diagram (build). WON: one input, one striking output, weekend-sized, rides the teardown-SVG primitive. 2) Proofline — evidence pack for agent-written PRs (venture). Runner-up: real pain from the Thorsten Ball article, but Cursor and Momentic already occupy parts of it. 3) Skill X-ray for `npx skills add` (build). DROPPED: repeat of Skillscope in the library. 4) Diligence answer drafter off the Papermark Data Rooms 2.0 launch (venture). DROPPED: repeat of Dossier. 5) Shadow-AI detector for abliterated/uncensored model endpoints, off the DeepSeek-V4.1 abliterated post (venture). DROPPED: Harmonic Security, Vorlon and the whole AI-SASE category already sell shadow-AI discovery to CISOs; a solo builder has no wedge and no distribution to security buyers. 6) "Hey Grok"-style voice shortcut pack (build). DROPPED: the bookmark is already the product, it is a config recipe not code, and there is nothing to ship.
research_notes: 6 searches and 3 summaries used. Summarised the agent-skills ecosystem (confirmed `npx skills add` is an open CLI standard, ~1M published skills reported by Anthropic in Oct 2026 — that is publisher-reported, not active users), Papermark Data Rooms 2.0 (€99/mo entry, open core with enterprise licence for commercial self-hosting), and the Thorsten Ball X article (key point: demand end-to-end proof from agents, record failures in AGENTS.md). I could not see any of the videos in the bookmarks, so I judged those posts only on their text. Searches changed two things: prior-art search for photo-to-assembly-instructions surfaced BILT (enterprise 3D work instructions) and iFixit but nothing that takes a user's own photo and returns a labelled exploded diagram — that kept Partsy alive and sharpened its wedge toward "name the part so you can buy it". A search on agent-PR verification surfaced Arize's write-up that Cursor already uses video evidence and risk scores internally, plus Momentic's evidence-based AI QA — that knocked Proofline from lead to runner-up. A shadow-AI search surfaced Harmonic Security and Vorlon, closing the gap on the abliterated-model governance idea, which I dropped.
prototype_summary: Partsy prototype: tap a sample object photo and watch it resolve into an animated, labelled exploded SVG diagram with a numbered parts list and copyable search terms.
